editorial.headline: Stadium Facilities: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Stadium facilities and self-run sports schools are nationally open to full foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium leaves no registration route at a Bali address.
editorial.body:
For a foreign investor, the Bali position is blunt: Stadium Facilities cannot be registered as PMA at a Bali address today. Nationally, the activity is open to foreign investment and permits up to 100 percent foreign ownership; in Bali, however, the record marks it closed under the province-wide PMA moratorium. This is not a marginal qualification to an otherwise open activity. The national setting and the Bali address rule lead to different outcomes, and a proposal that is available to fully foreign-owned investment nationally has no currently registrable PMA route in Bali.

Stadium Facilities is a venue-and-facilities activity, defined by the provision of places and infrastructure for sport as the principal business. The stated sports are football, hockey, cricket, baseball, jai-alai and athletics. The athletics scope expressly embraces running, throwing, jumping and related events, keeping the description anchored in the practical provision of a sporting setting. It also reaches self-managed schools or sports education in those same disciplines. In other words, the record places both the facilities and independently operated training or school activity for its named sports within this single field, provided they are managed by the operator itself.

Registration is open across the small, medium and large scales listed in the record. At the national level, “open” carries a concrete ownership consequence: the ceiling for foreign ownership is 100 percent, under the Presidential Regulations cited in the record. A foreign investor considering the activity outside the Bali restriction can therefore read the national setting plainly: full foreign ownership is permitted at that level. The classification does not, on its own, establish anything further about permits, timing or commercial arrangements; its significance here is the declared national access and ownership ceiling.

Bali applies a separate test. The record says that, notwithstanding national openness, the large scale is classified Medium-Low and is therefore caught by the Bali PMA moratorium. That provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration island-wide, and it is identified as permanent. The record traces the block to a gubernatorial letter dated May 13, 2026. This leaves no useful ambiguity for a Bali address: the 100 percent national ceiling describes the national position, while the Bali moratorium prevents PMA registration there.
